title: Wet shirt on clothesline

input: After washing his single white linen shirt by hand, Yusuf wrings it out and pins it to a clothesline strung between two posts in his sunny back garden on a warm, breezy summer afternoon. He then goes inside to read for several hours. No rain falls, no sprinkler runs, and no one touches the shirt while he is gone. In the early evening he steps back outside and takes the shirt down from the line.

must_identify: sun and wind cause water to evaporate
no new source of water added
hours of exposure is ample drying time
shirt has lost moisture

title: Ball rolled off ramp
question: After leaving the bottom of the ramp, does the ball continue moving across the floor, or stop instantly? Answer in one short phrase.
input: In her garage workshop, Ingrid props a smooth wooden plank against a sturdy chair to make a ramp. She places a heavy rubber ball at the top of the ramp, holds it still for a moment, then lets go. The ramp surface is clean and level along its width, the floor at the bottom of the ramp is bare polished concrete, and there is at least four meters of clear space in front of the ramp before any wall.

must_identify: gravity accelerates the ball down the ramp
objects in motion keep moving until friction stops them
smooth concrete offers little immediate resistance
ball rolls onward across the floor

title: Vampire bat species claim
question: Is the captured bat a member of family Desmodontidae? Answer yes or no.
input: Zoology reference: 'Every member of the family Desmodontidae feeds exclusively on blood and possesses heat-sensing pit organs around the nose.' A captured bat is brought to the lab. Examination shows it has no pit organs around its nose. Its fangs are sharp and it was found near livestock, but stomach contents include insect fragments alongside some blood traces, and its wing morphology resembles Desmodontidae.

must_identify: membership requires both blood-only diet and pit organs
absence of pit organs negates a required consequent feature
insect fragments also negate the exclusive-blood feeding requirement
wing morphology and livestock proximity are distractors
modus tollens denies family membership

title: Notarized contract validity
question: Is the contract legally binding under section 12? Answer yes or no.
input: Civil code section 12: 'A real estate contract is legally binding only if it bears the signatures of both parties and an embossed notary seal dated the same day as the signatures.' The disputed contract for the Maple Street property shows both signatures dated April 12th and an embossed notary seal also dated April 12th. The property buyer later claimed coercion, and the seller's attorney was disbarred two years after the signing.

must_identify: binding requires both signatures and matching-date notary seal
all required elements are present in the contract
coercion claim and later disbarment are distractors irrelevant to section 12
the rule's consequent is satisfied, so no modus tollens denial; binding stands

title: Star classification spectrum
question: Is HD-22841 a main-sequence O-class star? Answer yes or no.
input: Astrophysics text: 'If a star is on the main sequence and of spectral class O, then its spectrum exhibits prominent ionized helium absorption lines at 4541 and 4686 angstroms.' Spectroscopic observation of star HD-22841 shows no detectable absorption lines at either 4541 or 4686 angstroms; the spectrum instead shows strong hydrogen Balmer lines. The star is bright, blue-white in color, and was previously catalogued as a candidate hot star.

must_identify: conditional links main-sequence O class to ionized helium lines at 4541/4686
those lines are absent in HD-22841's spectrum
blue-white color and prior catalogue status are distractors
modus tollens denies main-sequence O classification

title: Murder weapon ballistic match
question: Did the suspect's revolver fire the scene bullet? Answer yes or no.
input: Forensic protocol: 'If a recovered firearm fired the bullet found at a crime scene, then microscopic comparison of the test-fired bullet and the scene bullet must show matching striation patterns on the lands and grooves.' Detective Vance submits the suspect's revolver for testing. The lab reports that the striation patterns on the test-fired bullet differ markedly from those on the scene bullet. The revolver is the same caliber as the scene bullet and was found in the suspect's car.

must_identify: firing implies matching striation patterns
lab reports striations do not match
matching caliber and location are distractors
modus tollens rules out the revolver as the source

title: Vaccine cold chain integrity
question: Does vial 4421 retain full potency? Answer yes or no.
input: Pharmaceutical guideline: 'A vial of VaxR retains full potency only if its temperature has remained between 2°C and 8°C continuously from manufacture to administration, as verified by an unbroken sequence of compliant readings on its attached digital logger.' Clinic nurse Adaeze examines a shipment and finds that vial 4421's logger records a four-hour interval at 11.3°C during transit last Wednesday. The vial's expiration date is still six months away and its physical seal appears intact.

must_identify: full potency requires continuous 2–8°C temperature record
logger shows 11.3°C for four hours, breaking the consequent
expiration date and intact seal are distractors
modus tollens denies full potency

title: Magma chamber and uplift
question: Will the GPS array record measurable surface uplift?
input: Volcanology textbook: If a magma chamber pressurizes above 200 MPa, it injects dikes into the surrounding crust. Whenever dikes are injected into the upper crust, GPS stations within 5 km record measurable surface uplift. Seismic swarms typically accompany pressurization, but the surface signal does not depend on swarm count. The Caldera Verde chamber reached 240 MPa last Tuesday, and a GPS array sits 3 km from the vent.

must_identify: pressure over 200 MPa implies dike injection
dike injection implies measurable GPS uplift within 5 km
Caldera Verde conditions trigger chain
seismic swarm note is a distractor

title: Citizenship transitive query
question: Is Ravi granted full citizenship?
input: Naturalization law: If an applicant has resided continuously in the country for ten years, they qualify for permanent resident status. Any permanent resident who passes the civics examination is granted full citizenship. A separate fast-track exists for spouses of citizens, requiring only three years of residence. Applicant Ravi has lived in the country continuously for twelve years, is unmarried, and passed the civics examination last month.

must_identify: ten years continuous residence implies permanent resident status
permanent resident plus civics pass implies full citizenship
Ravi meets both conditions
spousal fast-track is a distractor

title: Server outage cascade
question: Will the analytics pipeline experience at least four hours of stale data?
input: DevOps runbook: If the primary database node loses quorum, then read-replicas are promoted to handle writes. Whenever read-replicas handle writes, the analytics pipeline experiences at least four hours of stale data. The monitoring dashboard, separately, will display a yellow banner during any planned maintenance window. This morning at 03:00, the primary database node lost quorum due to a network partition; no maintenance was scheduled.

must_identify: quorum loss implies replica promotion for writes
replica writes imply 4+ hours stale analytics
this morning's outage triggers chain
yellow banner rule is a distractor

title: Patent grant chain
question: Will Lim's application be granted a patent within 60 days of clearing obviousness review?
input: Patent office rules: If an application passes the novelty examination, it advances to the obviousness review. Any application that clears the obviousness review is granted a patent within 60 days. The office also runs a separate design-patent track with different criteria. Inventor Lim's utility application for a new battery electrolyte passed the novelty examination in March and cleared the obviousness review in April. She has not filed any design patents.

must_identify: novelty pass implies obviousness review
obviousness clearance implies patent grant within 60 days
Lim cleared obviousness in April
design-patent track is a distractor

title: Hormone signaling chain
question: Will GLUT4 transporters translocate to Tomas's muscle cell membranes?
input: Endocrinology lecture: If circulating glucose remains above 180 mg/dL for thirty minutes, pancreatic beta cells release insulin into the bloodstream. Whenever insulin reaches skeletal muscle tissue via the bloodstream, GLUT4 transporters translocate to muscle cell membranes. A separate pathway involving glucagon governs liver glycogen breakdown during fasting. After a heavy meal, subject Tomas showed a sustained blood glucose of 210 mg/dL for forty-five minutes; he had not been fasting.

must_identify: sustained high glucose implies insulin release
insulin in bloodstream implies GLUT4 translocation
Tomas's 210 mg/dL for 45 min triggers chain
glucagon pathway is a distractor

title: Rover signal loss reason
question: What caused the signal loss?
input: Mission control determined that the Mars rover lost contact due to either an antenna misalignment or a solar-panel power drop — telemetry from the previous orbit narrowed root causes to these two subsystems. Engineers had earlier flagged a software memory leak, but a patch deployed weeks ago resolved it and it is no longer a candidate cause. The latest reacquired data shows the antenna is correctly oriented within tolerance.

must_identify: two-subsystem exhaustive disjunction
memory leak is a distractor (already patched)
antenna misalignment eliminated by orientation data
solar-panel power drop remains

title: Treaty ratification outcome
question: How was the treaty ratified?
input: Constitutional rules state that the treaty becomes law only if ratified by either the Senate or a national referendum; no other path to ratification exists. Commentators speculated that an executive decree might suffice, but the constitution explicitly forbids that route. Today the Senate voted on the treaty and the motion to ratify failed, with the chamber rejecting the treaty by a clear margin. The treaty is, however, now law.

must_identify: two-path exhaustive ratification disjunction
executive decree is a distractor (forbidden)
Senate ratification eliminated by failed vote
national referendum is the remaining path

title: Garden pest culprit
question: What caused the damage?
input: The gardener concluded that the damage to the cabbage patch came from either slugs or cabbage loopers; field guides for the region list only these two pests capable of producing this leaf-edge damage pattern. A neighbor suggested rabbits, but the patch is enclosed by rabbit-proof fencing. After a thorough nighttime inspection with traps and a flashlight, no slugs or slug trails were found anywhere in or around the cabbage patch.

must_identify: two-pest exhaustive disjunction
rabbits are a distractor (fencing excludes them)
slugs eliminated by inspection
cabbage loopers remain

title: Verdict logic puzzle
question: What was the verdict? Answer in two words.
input: The judge's instructions state that the jury must return either a guilty verdict or a not-guilty verdict; under this jurisdiction's rules a hung jury is not an available outcome and verdicts must be unanimous. A spectator hoped for a mistrial, but the judge has ruled out a mistrial earlier in proceedings. The court clerk has just announced that the jury did not find the defendant guilty.

must_identify: two-verdict exhaustive disjunction
mistrial is a distractor (ruled out)
guilty eliminated by clerk's announcement
not guilty remains

title: Funding source remaining
question: Which source will fund the program?
input: The nonprofit's treasurer reports that the new program's budget will be covered by either the Hartwell Grant or the Endicott Foundation award — board policy restricts large-program funding to these two approved sources this fiscal year. A donor offered a personal pledge, but the board declined to count individual pledges toward program budgets. The Hartwell Grant committee notified the nonprofit yesterday that its application has been formally rejected.

must_identify: two-source exhaustive funding disjunction
individual pledge is a distractor (declined by policy)
Hartwell Grant eliminated by rejection
Endicott Foundation award remains

title: Bakery preorder pickup slip
question: Did Tess place a preorder for the holiday box? Answer yes or no.
input: Maren's Bakery posts a notice: 'If a customer placed a preorder for the holiday box, then they received a numbered pink pickup slip at the time of ordering.' Customer Tess arrives on pickup day claiming she preordered a holiday box two weeks ago. She produces no pink slip and acknowledges she has no slip of any color; she insists the clerk simply forgot to give her one. Bakery records of slip distribution are complete and incorruptible — the slip system has been audited and never fails.

must_identify: notice conditional: preordered → received pink slip
Tess has no pink slip (consequent denied)
contrapositive: no slip → did not preorder
Tess's claim and 'clerk forgot' are distractors

title: Quantum lab access keycard
question: Did Wen enter the quantum lab between 22:00 and 06:00? Answer yes or no.
input: Facility rule: 'If a researcher entered the quantum lab between 22:00 and 06:00, then the access log records their keycard ID with a timestamp in that window.' Investigator Dahl pulls the complete, tamper-proof access log for last night and finds no entry whatsoever for researcher Wen between 22:00 and 06:00. A custodian recalls 'someone who looked like Wen' walking near the lab corridor around midnight, and Wen's office light was on at 23:30 according to a separate building log.

must_identify: rule: entered lab in window → keycard logged in window
no log entry for Wen in window (consequent denied)
contrapositive: not logged → did not enter
custodian sighting and office light are distractors

title: Wine vintage cork brand
question: Is this bottle from the 1987 Belrive vintage? Answer yes or no.
input: Château Belrive's records indicate: 'If a bottle is from the 1987 Belrive vintage, then its cork is branded with a small fleur-de-lis above the year.' Sommelier Orin examines a bottle the seller claims is a 1987 Belrive. He extracts the cork carefully and finds it branded only with the year and the château name — no fleur-de-lis appears anywhere on the cork. The label, capsule, and bottle shape all appear consistent with the era, and the seller provides a provenance certificate from a reputable auction house.

must_identify: records conditional: 1987 vintage → fleur-de-lis on cork
cork lacks fleur-de-lis (consequent denied)
contrapositive: no fleur-de-lis → not 1987 vintage
label and provenance are distractors

title: Software build artifact hash
question: Was build-2041.tar produced by the official CI pipeline? Answer yes or no.
input: DevOps standard: 'If a build artifact was produced by the official CI pipeline, then it appears in the signed manifest with a SHA-256 hash matching the artifact's contents.' Engineer Pria computes the SHA-256 of artifact build-2041.tar and searches the signed manifest. The manifest contains no entry whose hash matches her computed value, and no entry naming build-2041.tar at all. The artifact was found in the deployment bucket and its filename matches the project's CI naming convention exactly.

must_identify: standard: CI-produced → in signed manifest with matching hash
no matching manifest entry (consequent denied)
contrapositive: not in manifest → not CI-produced
naming convention and bucket location are distractors

title: Guild apprentice bell rule
question: Has Joren been formally accepted into the guild? Answer yes or no.
input: Stonecutters' Guild custom dictates: 'If an apprentice has been formally accepted into the guild, then their name has been rung on the brass bell during the monthly induction ceremony.' Master Kael reviews the bell-ringing records, which the bellkeeper maintains under oath and which have never been incomplete. The records show no ringing of apprentice Joren's name at any induction ceremony, past or present. Joren wears the gray apron commonly worn by apprentices and has been seen working in the guild courtyard for several weeks.

must_identify: custom: formally accepted → name rung on bell
Joren's name never rung (consequent denied)
contrapositive: not rung → not formally accepted
apron and courtyard work are distractors

title: Online forum debate moderation
question: Is Lin's response in the policy thread an ad hominem fallacy? Answer yes or no.
input: User Argo posts that the moderation policy unfairly auto-flags posts containing the word 'kill' regardless of context, citing 12 examples of cooking-related posts being removed. Moderator Lin replies in a separate thread that Argo is annoying and posts too often. In the actual policy thread, Lin writes: 'The keyword filter triggers on 'kill' without parsing context, which is why your cooking examples were caught. We're rolling out a contextual classifier next week.'

must_identify: Argo's claim concerns auto-flagging and 12 examples
the insult occurs in a separate thread, not as rebuttal
the policy-thread reply engages the substantive issue
mere insults outside the rebuttal context don't qualify
the actual rebuttal addresses the claim

title: Historian methodology challenge
question: Is Holm's response an ad hominem fallacy? Answer yes or no.
input: Dr. Castellan argues that 19th-century industrial wage data has been systematically misread because researchers ignored regional in-kind compensation. He presents archival ledgers from four mill towns showing 18-25% of compensation was non-monetary. Critic Holm replies: 'Castellan is a known revisionist with an axe to grind against orthodox economic history. His ideological commitments make his work unreliable.' Holm publishes no analysis of the ledgers or the in-kind percentages.

must_identify: Castellan's claim rests on archival ledgers and 18-25% figure
Holm attacks ideological commitments
the ledger evidence is unaddressed
label of 'revisionist' substitutes for engagement

title: Product safety hearing reply
question: Is Reeves's response an ad hominem fallacy? Answer yes or no.
input: Engineer Sato testifies that the children's car seat fails federal side-impact standards in 4 of 10 lab tests, citing crash-test footage and force readings exceeding 80g at the head. Company spokesperson Reeves replies: 'These tests came from Sato's lab. Specifically, his rig uses a fixed sled rather than the rotating sled the federal standard now permits, which inflates measured g-forces. Re-running with rotation gives readings under threshold.'

must_identify: Sato's claim is 4-of-10 failures and 80g readings
Reeves identifies a specific methodological issue (fixed vs rotating sled)
Reeves engages the substantive evidence
this is a methodology rebuttal, not a personal attack

title: Editorial board exchange
question: Is Marsh's response an ad hominem fallacy? Answer yes or no.
input: Columnist Devi writes that the city's homeless count undercounts by roughly 30% because it relies on a single-night street survey and excludes those couch-surfing or in vehicles. She cites comparison studies from three peer cities. Editor Marsh responds in print: 'Devi is young, idealistic, and clearly emotionally invested in this cause. Readers should weigh her piece accordingly.' Marsh offers no discussion of the 30% estimate, the survey method, or the peer-city comparisons.

must_identify: Devi's claims rest on the 30% figure and peer comparisons
Marsh attacks age and emotional state
the survey methodology is unaddressed
personal traits used to discount the argument

title: Two responses ranked
question: Which response is the clearer ad hominem fallacy, A or B?
input: Researcher Quinn presents data that a popular supplement showed no effect over placebo in a 600-person trial (p=0.71). Response A: 'Quinn used a 12-week protocol, but the supplement's manufacturer recommends 16 weeks for effect; the trial was underpowered to detect the actual mechanism.' Response B: 'Quinn is funded by a pharmaceutical rival and has tweeted dismissively about supplements before; nothing she says about this industry can be trusted.' Both responses reject Quinn's conclusion.

must_identify: Quinn's claim is null effect at p=0.71 in 600-person trial
Response A engages duration and power substantively
Response B targets funding and prior tweets without engaging the trial
B fits both ad hominem criteria, A does not

title: Request for clarification
question: Did Ruiz commit a straw-man fallacy? Answer yes or no.
input: Professor Aoki: 'Departments should require a brief preregistration document for any study involving human subjects before data collection.' Colleague Ruiz: 'To make sure I understand — are you proposing this only for human-subjects research, or would it also apply to archival meta-analyses and computational simulations? I want to know the scope before responding.' Ruiz asks rather than asserts and offers no rebuttal yet.

must_identify: Aoki's claim concerned human-subjects research preregistration
Ruiz did not restate or attack a distorted version
Ruiz asked for clarification on scope
Clarification requests are excluded by the procedure

title: Telework pilot program
question: What fallacy did Calder commit?
input: HR Director Pham: 'I propose a six-month pilot allowing engineering staff to work remotely two days per week, with quarterly check-ins on productivity.' VP Calder: 'Pham wants to abolish the office and have everyone work from home permanently. Office culture is the heart of our company, and dismantling it would destroy morale.' Calder spends the meeting defending in-office culture against full remote work. Pham's proposal preserved three in-office days and was time-limited.

must_identify: Pham proposed a six-month pilot, two remote days, with check-ins
Calder restated it as abolishing the office and permanent full remote
Calder attacked the abolish-the-office version
Pham never endorsed full remote or eliminating the office

title: Two paraphrases ranked
question: Which paraphrase is the straw man — X or Y?
input: Speaker Ortega: 'City permits for outdoor amplified music in residential parks should end at 9pm on weeknights.' Paraphrase X (by Critic Lim): 'Ortega wants to silence all music in public spaces — a war on artistic expression.' Lim then attacks Ortega for opposing public art. Paraphrase Y (by Critic Brand): 'Ortega proposes a 9pm weeknight cutoff for amplified music in residential parks. I disagree because community concerts often run until 9:30pm.' Brand engages the actual cutoff time and venue.

must_identify: Ortega's claim was narrow: 9pm weeknights, amplified, residential parks
Paraphrase X broadened it to silencing all music in public spaces
Paraphrase X attacked the broadened version
Paraphrase Y preserved scope and engaged the actual claim

title: Drug policy nuance
question: Did Walsh commit a straw-man fallacy? Answer yes or no.
input: Public health official Dr. Nair: 'We should decriminalize possession of small personal-use quantities of cannabis while maintaining penalties for trafficking and sales to minors.' Commentator Walsh: 'Nair wants to legalize all drugs for everyone, including selling heroin to children. This reckless agenda will devastate communities.' Walsh proceeds to argue against legalizing all drugs and selling to children. Nair's proposal explicitly excluded trafficking, sales to minors, and other substances.

must_identify: Nair's claim was narrow: small cannabis possession, with explicit exclusions
Walsh recast it as legalizing all drugs and selling to children
Walsh attacked the broadened, distorted version
Nair explicitly preserved penalties for trafficking and minor sales

title: Strong tone, faithful content
question: Did Krause commit a straw-man fallacy? Answer yes or no.
input: Architect Bellweather: 'New construction in the historic district should be limited to four stories to preserve sightlines from the riverfront promenade.' Developer Krause snaps: 'This is absurd and economically illiterate. Bellweather is proposing a four-story cap on new construction in the historic district to preserve riverfront sightlines. I think it's wrong because land values demand at least six stories to pencil out, and the sightline concern can be addressed with setback rules instead.' Krause is hostile but represents the proposal accurately.

must_identify: Bellweather's claim was a four-story cap in the historic district for sightline reasons
Krause's restatement preserved scope, height, district, and rationale
Krause's rebuttal engaged the actual proposal with economic and alternative arguments
Hostile tone alone does not constitute a straw man per the procedure

title: Diet book introduction
question: Does the book's framing restrict the choice space through a false dilemma? Answer yes or no.
input: The bestseller's first chapter announced: 'You have two choices. You can adopt strict carnivore eating starting tomorrow, or you can resign yourself to chronic inflammation, fatigue, and early death. Mediterranean, vegetarian, and balanced approaches have all been tried and all failed at the population level. Forget moderation — moderation is what got us here. Pick the carnivore path or pick decline.'

must_identify: the binary is 'carnivore diet' vs 'chronic illness and death'
many viable dietary alternatives exist (Mediterranean, plant-based, balanced)
the book mentions but dismisses them without specific evidence
a wide spectrum of nutritional approaches is collapsed

title: Climate policy editorial
question: Does the editorial's framing restrict the choice space through a false dilemma? Answer yes or no.
input: An editorial argued: 'The climate question reduces to one decision: ban all fossil fuel use within five years, or accept catastrophic warming. Carbon pricing schemes, gradual transitions, renewable buildouts, and efficiency programs have been tried for decades and have produced nothing. The window for half-measures has closed. It's prohibition or planetary disaster — there is no third path.'

must_identify: the binary is 'five-year fossil fuel ban' vs 'catastrophic warming'
intermediate policies exist (carbon pricing, phased transitions, efficiency)
the editorial dismisses them rhetorically rather than with specific evidence
a policy spectrum is compressed into two extremes

title: Coin toss outcome
question: Does the referee's framing restrict the choice space through a false dilemma? Answer yes or no.
input: The referee explained the protocol: 'Before kickoff, I'll toss a fair coin. The visiting captain calls it in the air. Once it lands flat on the turf, the upward face will be either heads or tails. If it lands on edge — which has effectively zero probability on grass — we re-toss. So the recorded outcome of any completed toss is one of those two faces, and that determines who chooses to receive.'

must_identify: the binary is heads vs tails on a completed toss
the edge case is explicitly acknowledged and handled
the two outcomes are practically exhaustive given the protocol
no viable alternative is being rhetorically suppressed

title: Startup founder's pivot
question: Does the founder's framing restrict the choice space through a false dilemma? Answer yes or no.
input: The founder told investors: 'We must either pivot to enterprise sales immediately, or shut down by June. Continuing the consumer freemium model is not on the table — the unit economics are broken. I know some of you will ask about hybrid go-to-market, prosumer tiers, or partnerships, but the runway math is clear and brutal: enterprise pivot or wind-down. I need your sign-off this week.' The pitch deck contained no financial breakdown of hybrid options.

must_identify: the binary is 'enterprise pivot' vs 'shutdown'
the founder names alternatives (hybrid, prosumer, partnerships) but doesn't analyze them
no financial justification is provided for ruling them out
plausible middle paths exist in startup strategy

title: Jury verdict instruction
question: Does the judge's framing restrict the choice space through a false dilemma? Answer yes or no.
input: The judge instructed the jury: 'On the single charge before you, your verdict must be unanimous and must be one of two: guilty or not guilty. The court does not accept partial verdicts on this charge, and any nuance about the defendant's degree of involvement should be reflected in your deliberations rather than in a third verdict option, because no third option exists under the statute governing this offense. If you cannot reach unanimity, report a hung jury.'

must_identify: the binary is guilty vs not guilty on the single charge
the statute genuinely makes these exhaustive
the hung-jury possibility is explicitly acknowledged
the framing is justified by legal procedure, not rhetorical compression

title: Marijuana legalization analyst
question: Does this passage commit a slippery-slope fallacy? Answer yes or no.
input: A drug policy analyst writes: 'Legalizing recreational marijuana in Colorado was followed by a measurable increase in adult use, documented in the 2018 RAND assessment showing a rise from 13% to 17% past-month use among adults aged 21+. The same report found no statistically significant change in adolescent use rates over the same period.' The analyst presents only these documented findings.

must_identify: only documented past consequences, not predicted chain
specific evidence (RAND, percentages) cited
no escalating predictions of catastrophe
empirical reporting is not the fallacy

title: Compare two arguments
question: Which argument commits the slippery-slope fallacy, A or B?
input: Argument A: 'If we cap rents, landlords will defer maintenance. Deferred maintenance leads to housing decay. Housing decay drives families out. Families leaving causes neighborhood collapse. Neighborhood collapse spreads citywide. Eventually the entire metro becomes uninhabitable.' No evidence is cited. Argument B: 'If we cap rents at 3% annual growth, landlord profit margins will compress, as shown in the Diamond-McQuade-Qian (2019) San Francisco study, which documented a 15% reduction in rental housing supply over a decade.'

must_identify: Argument A has 5+ escalating steps with no evidence
Argument A endpoint (uninhabitable metro) disproportionate
Argument B cites specific study for its single claim
only A meets both criteria for the fallacy

title: Vaccine mandate trap
question: Does this commentator commit a slippery-slope fallacy? Answer yes or no.
input: A commentator writes: 'A measles vaccine mandate for kindergarten enrollment is reasonable. CDC surveillance data from 1980-2019 shows that school-entry mandates correlate with sustained measles vaccination rates above 95%, the threshold for herd immunity per epidemiological modeling by Fine (1993). States that relaxed mandates, such as California pre-SB277, saw vaccination rates fall below this threshold and experienced documented outbreaks.' The argument stops there.

must_identify: argument cites CDC surveillance and epidemiological modeling
specific historical example (California SB277) provided
no chain of escalating unsupported predictions
controversial topic is a trap; evidence determines fallacy status

title: Locate unsupported transition
question: Does this pundit's overall argument commit a slippery-slope fallacy? Answer yes or no.
input: A pundit argues: 'A 1% wealth tax on billionaires will trigger capital flight (a 2020 OECD study found measurable but small migration responses to wealth taxes, around 0.01% of taxpayers per percentage point). Capital flight will then crash the stock market. A market crash will cause mass unemployment. Mass unemployment will trigger civil unrest, and ultimately, the dissolution of the federal government.' Only the first link cites evidence.

must_identify: first transition is supported but subsequent ones are not
chain has 4+ escalating steps after the cited one
final endpoint (federal dissolution) disproportionate
partial citation does not rescue an otherwise unsupported chain

title: Counting the links
question: Does this blog post commit a slippery-slope fallacy? Answer yes or no.
input: A blogger writes: 'If we ban plastic straws, restaurants will switch to paper. Paper straws disintegrate in drinks, frustrating customers.' No further consequences are predicted. The blogger does not cite studies but makes only this two-step claim about a tangible mechanism.

must_identify: only two steps, not three or more escalating
no disproportionate catastrophic endpoint
a stated mechanism (disintegration) is offered
fails the escalation-pattern requirement of the fallacy

title: Teacher with strong evidence
question: Does this passage demonstrate confirmation bias? Answer yes or no.
input: Mr. Alvarez believes Priya is the strongest math student in his class. The school's standardized exam, the state competition, three pop quizzes, and her two semester finals all place her at the top by a clear margin. Alvarez also tracks his other students with the same metrics; Priya's lead is consistent across every measure. He has reviewed the lower-scoring students' work for any sign he has missed talent and found nothing comparable. His belief is based on the full distribution of evidence, not selective sampling.

must_identify: prior belief is correct and well-supported
evidence gathered symmetrically across students
strong evidence alone is not confirmation bias
no asymmetric attention demonstrated

title: Historian's favored thesis
question: Identify the reasoning flaw. Answer in two words.
input: Professor Harlan argues the 1840 famine was caused primarily by export policy. In his book he cites four shipping ledgers showing grain leaving the country. He devotes one footnote to the contemporaneous potato blight and dismisses it as 'incidental.' Three peer-reviewed studies estimating the blight caused 70% of crop loss are absent from his bibliography. When a colleague raises them, Harlan replies 'those authors have ideological commitments.' He has not engaged with their data. For the 1845 famine, which he does not have a thesis about, he discusses blight extensively.

must_identify: prior thesis (export policy caused famine)
selective citation of supporting ledgers
ignored/dismissed disconfirming blight studies
asymmetric treatment between 1840 and 1845 cases

title: Engineer debugging the system
question: Does this engineer demonstrate confirmation bias? Answer yes or no.
input: Engineer Yu suspects the database is the bottleneck. She profiles the database and finds query latency at 40ms. She also profiles the application server (12ms), the network (3ms), and the cache layer (180ms — far higher than expected). She updates her hypothesis: the cache, not the database, is the primary bottleneck. She writes a postmortem noting her initial guess was wrong and explains how the cache miss rate, which she had not initially considered, drove the slowdown. She implements a cache fix and latency drops by 70%.

must_identify: prior hypothesis (database bottleneck)
she gathered evidence on all components
she updated when disconfirming evidence appeared
belief revision in light of evidence is the opposite of the bias

title: Parent and the bad influence friend
question: Does Mrs. Cole demonstrate confirmation bias? Answer yes or no.
input: Mrs. Cole has decided her son's friend Dani is a bad influence. She mentions to her husband every time her son comes home late after seeing Dani, but not the times he comes home late after seeing other friends. She remembers Dani once swore in front of her, but has forgotten the same swear-word incident from her son's friend Theo. When her son's grades drop in a semester he barely sees Dani, she still blames Dani's 'lingering effect.' When his grades rose last year while he saw Dani daily, she attributes it to a new tutor.

must_identify: prior belief Dani is a bad influence
selective memory of Dani's transgressions vs Theo's
reinterpreting disconfirming timing of grade changes
asymmetric attribution

title: Two analysts, one report
question: Which analyst exhibits confirmation bias, A or B?
input: Analyst A and Analyst B both write memos on whether Country X will default. A starts with the view that default is likely. She lists rising bond yields, falling reserves, and political instability — all consistent with her view. She does not mention the recent IMF agreement or the upturn in export revenue, both of which appear in the same dataset. B starts with the same prior but lists the bond yields, reserves, instability, AND the IMF deal and exports, then weighs them, concluding default is moderately likely. Which analyst exhibits confirmation bias?

must_identify: both analysts hold the same prior
A cites only supporting evidence
A omits available disconfirming evidence (IMF deal, exports)
B engages with both sides symmetrically

title: Jury damages suggestion
question: Was the jury award distorted by anchoring? Answer yes or no.
input: In a civil suit, the plaintiff's attorney requests $50 million in damages during opening statements, a figure she later admits in chambers was 'a starting number to plant in jurors' minds.' The jury awards $14 million. Comparable verdicts for similar injuries in the same jurisdiction over the past five years averaged $2.5 million.

must_identify: the $50 million request was strategically chosen, not analytically derived
comparable verdicts averaged $2.5 million
jurors' figure was framed relative to the request
the award was pulled upward toward the anchor

title: Patient pain rating context
question: Does this passage demonstrate anchoring bias? Answer yes or no.
input: A nurse asks a patient, 'On a 0-10 scale, where 10 is the worst pain imaginable, how would you rate your pain?' The patient responds '6.' The nurse documents the rating using the standard validated pain scale used hospital-wide. No reference to other patients' ratings or specific numbers was made before the question.

must_identify: the 0-10 scale endpoints are a legitimate measurement framework, not arbitrary anchors
no prior reference number was used to bias the patient
the rating was given on a standardized validated scale
this is a legitimate benchmark, not anchoring

title: Real estate flip pricing
question: Was the buyer's offer distorted by anchoring? Answer yes or no.
input: A flipper bought a house for $310,000 and lists it at $625,000 after renovations. A buyer offers $580,000, describing it as 'well below ask.' Three nearby renovated homes of similar size and finish sold in the past two months for $440,000, $455,000, and $462,000. The flipper had set the list price by 'doubling what I paid plus a bit.'

must_identify: the $625,000 list price was set arbitrarily (double purchase price)
comparable renovated sales were $440,000-$462,000
the offer was evaluated as 'below ask' rather than against comparables
the offer was pulled upward toward the inflated list

title: Engineering tolerance estimate
question: Was the engineer's estimate distorted by anchoring? Answer yes or no.
input: An engineer is asked to estimate the load capacity of a new bridge design. A junior colleague mentions in passing, 'The old bridge was rated at 80 tons.' The engineer ignores this, runs finite element analysis on the new design's geometry and materials, applies standard safety factors, and reports a capacity of 134 tons. Her calculations are independently audited and confirmed.

must_identify: the 80-ton figure preceded the estimate
the engineer used independent finite element analysis
her result (134 tons) is far from the mentioned anchor
the audit confirmed the independent derivation

title: Discount sticker grocery item
question: Was the shopper's purchase judgment distorted by anchoring? Answer yes or no.
input: A store sticker reads 'Was $19.99, Now $9.99!' A shopper buys the item, satisfied with the 50% savings. A consumer watchdog later reveals the item never actually sold at $19.99; the 'was' price was printed only to make the current price look like a deal. Other stores routinely sell the identical item for $7.50 to $8.00.

must_identify: the $19.99 'was' price was fabricated and never real
competitors sell the item for $7.50-$8.00
the shopper evaluated $9.99 as a discount from $19.99
the judgment was pulled by an arbitrary anchor

title: Politician on gambling regulation
question: What fallacy does the pundit commit?
input: Representative Schultz argues that online sports gambling should be more tightly regulated because addiction rates among users have tripled in three years according to state health data. A pundit replies: 'Schultz placed bets on three NFL games last Sunday — public records prove it. He's the last person who should lecture us about gambling. His bill deserves no consideration.' The pundit doesn't address the addiction statistics.

must_identify: original claim cites addiction statistics
pundit attacks Schultz's own gambling
inconsistency used to reject the bill
statistics go unaddressed

title: Lawyer's perjury cross-examination
question: Does the prosecutor's challenge commit the tu quoque fallacy? Answer yes or no.
input: On the witness stand, defendant Hollis testifies under oath: 'I have always been completely honest in my business dealings.' The prosecutor cross-examines: 'Mr. Hollis, in 2019 you signed three invoices certifying delivery of goods you knew had not shipped. In 2021 you submitted a falsified expense report. Your claim of consistent honesty is contradicted by your own documented dishonesty.' The prosecutor uses these acts to undermine the testimony's truth.

must_identify: Hollis's claim is specifically about his own honesty
his conduct is itself the evidence at issue
challenging that conduct directly tests the claim
this is relevant character evidence, not tu quoque

title: Author on social media use
question: Does the reviewer's reply commit the tu quoque fallacy? Answer yes or no.
input: Author Beatrice publishes a book arguing that constant social media use erodes attention spans, citing neuroscience research on dopamine cycles and longitudinal studies of teen cognition. A reviewer writes: 'Beatrice posts on Twitter forty times a day. If her thesis were correct, she would have curtailed her own use. Her own behavior refutes her book.' The review never engages with the cited neuroscience or the longitudinal data.

must_identify: original claim rests on neuroscience and longitudinal evidence
reviewer targets Beatrice's posting behavior
hypocrisy treated as refutation of the thesis
cited evidence goes unaddressed

title: Two critics of fitness program
question: Which critic commits the tu quoque fallacy, X or Y?
input: Trainer Kalinda promotes a 30-day program, claiming participants average 8 pounds of fat loss based on her client data. Critic X says: 'Kalinda is overweight herself. Anyone who can't follow her own program has no business selling it — ignore her claim.' Critic Y says: 'Her client data lacks a control group; without one, we can't attribute the loss to her program rather than seasonal patterns.' Identify the fallacious one.

must_identify: X attacks Kalinda's body, not the data
X uses inconsistency as grounds for dismissal
Y engages substantively with study design
only X meets both fallacy elements

title: Pastor on charitable giving
question: What rhetorical fallacy is the congregant employing?
input: Pastor Idris preaches that congregants should tithe 10% of income, grounding the obligation in scriptural passages he interprets at length and in the church's documented community programs funded by tithes. A congregant objects: 'Pastor Idris drives a luxury car and vacations abroad. He clearly doesn't sacrifice as he asks us to. His sermon's demand is therefore void and we owe nothing.' The objection bypasses the scriptural exegesis and program data.

must_identify: original claim rests on scripture and program evidence
congregant attacks the pastor's lifestyle
perceived inconsistency used to void the obligation
the scriptural and program arguments are unaddressed

title: Free beer and free will
question: Which word is used equivocally?
input: A pamphleteer writes: 'Our tavern offers free beer to members. Free things have no constraints on them. Members' beer therefore has no constraints, meaning members may take unlimited quantities without restriction.' The pamphlet treats the inference as a straightforward consequence of the meaning of 'free'.

must_identify: 'free' appears in both premises
first 'free' means at no monetary cost
second 'free' means unconstrained or unrestricted
the unlimited-quantity conclusion depends on conflating the senses

title: Heavy reading material
question: Which word shifts meaning to support the conclusion?
input: A student complains: 'This book is heavy. Heavy things are hard to lift. Therefore, this book is hard to lift intellectually, which excuses my failure to finish the reading assignment.' The student presents this to the professor as a legitimate reason for an extension.

must_identify: 'heavy' appears in both premises
first 'heavy' refers to physical weight
second 'heavy' is reinterpreted as intellectually demanding
the excuse only works by sliding between physical and metaphorical senses

title: Hot peppers and hot stocks
question: Which word is the load-bearing equivocation?
input: An investor pitches: 'Jalapenos are hot. Hot items sell quickly on the market. Therefore, jalapenos sell quickly on the stock market, and we should add them to our trading portfolio as a high-velocity asset.' The pitch is delivered with charts showing both pepper sales and stock turnover.

must_identify: 'hot' appears in both premises
first 'hot' means spicy in flavor
second 'hot' means in high demand or trending
the portfolio recommendation depends on treating the two senses as identical

title: Critical thinking critically endangered
question: Which word equivocates between the premises?
input: An op-ed claims: 'Critical thinking is essential for civic life. Critical species are nearing extinction and require emergency intervention. Therefore, critical thinking is nearing extinction and requires emergency government intervention through mandatory programs in every workplace.' The op-ed treats the parallelism as an argument from shared category.

must_identify: 'critical' appears in both premises
first 'critical' means analytical or evaluative
second 'critical' means in a state of dire endangerment
the call for intervention rests on conflating the two senses

title: Knowing nothing for certain
question: Which phrase or word is used equivocally to generate the apparent contradiction?
input: A skeptic argues: 'Socrates knew that he knew nothing. Knowing nothing means having no knowledge whatsoever. Therefore, Socrates had no knowledge whatsoever, including no knowledge that he knew nothing, which contradicts the first premise and proves the whole tradition incoherent.' The skeptic offers this as a definitive refutation of Socratic philosophy.

must_identify: 'knew nothing' or 'nothing' appears in both premises
first occurrence means knowing one lacks certain wisdom (a specific epistemic claim)
second occurrence is read as having literally zero knowledge
the contradiction depends on collapsing the modest sense into the absolute sense

title: Product safety recall debate
question: Does the official's argument commit an appeal to emotion fallacy? Answer yes or no.
input: A consumer-protection official argues for a stroller recall: 'Seventeen infants have suffered skull fractures linked to the latch failure, documented in CPSC incident reports. The mechanism — a brittle plastic pin — fails in lab testing at 40% of advertised load. One mother described holding her unconscious baby in the ER, a moment no parent should face. We must recall.' The report includes photographs of the failed component alongside testing data.

must_identify: claim is that the stroller should be recalled
incident counts and lab test results are direct evidence
the mother's account supplements but does not replace data
removing the anecdote still leaves substantial evidence

title: Editorial on prison reform
question: Does the editorial commit an appeal to emotion fallacy? Answer yes or no.
input: An editorial opposes a sentencing-reduction bill: 'Imagine the family of a murder victim, lighting a candle each year on the anniversary, learning that their loved one's killer walks free a decade early. Picture the rage, the renewed grief, the sleepless nights. The bill's proponents speak of recidivism rates and budget savings, but those numbers cannot dry a single tear.' The editorial does not contest or analyze the cited recidivism or cost figures.

must_identify: claim is that the sentencing-reduction bill should be opposed
support is grief and anger of victims' families
the recidivism and cost evidence cited by proponents is dismissed without analysis
emotion is offered as a reason to disregard, not refute, evidence

title: Memorial fundraising letter
question: Does the letter commit an appeal to emotion fallacy? Answer yes or no.
input: A veterans' group writes: 'Our claim is simple: the lives lost at Belleau Wood deserve to be remembered, and grief among surviving families remains real a century later. We have collected 1,200 letters from descendants describing the lasting emotional weight of that loss. Please support our memorial maintenance fund so that this remembrance can continue.' The fundraising target is the upkeep of an existing memorial.

must_identify: the claim concerns the reality and persistence of grief and remembrance
emotion is the legitimate subject of the claim itself
the 1,200 letters constitute relevant evidence for that claim
the exception for emotion-as-subject applies

title: Tech regulation panel
question: Does the founder's testimony commit an appeal to emotion fallacy? Answer yes or no.
input: A startup founder testifying against a proposed data-privacy rule says: 'I built this company in my garage. My wife took a second job; I missed my daughter's first steps coding through the night. We employ 60 people now, each with their own story of sacrifice and hope. This rule would crush us. I beg you not to extinguish the American dream we represent.' He does not address the rule's compliance requirements, available exemptions for small firms, or estimated compliance costs.

must_identify: claim is that the privacy rule should not be adopted
support is personal sacrifice narrative and pride imagery
compliance specifics, exemptions, and costs are not analyzed
removing the emotional narrative leaves no argument against the rule

title: Hospital closure analysis
question: Does the analyst's argument commit an appeal to emotion fallacy? Answer yes or no.
input: A health-policy analyst opposes closing a rural hospital: 'The closure would force patients to travel an average of 47 additional miles for emergency care; published studies estimate this raises out-of-hospital cardiac mortality by roughly 8%. Last winter, an elderly farmer named Tom died in an ambulance during a long transfer — a death his family believes the closer hospital could have prevented. The mortality projections, not Tom's case alone, are why I oppose the closure.'

must_identify: claim is that the hospital should not be closed
distance and mortality estimates are direct evidence
Tom's story illustrates but is explicitly not the basis of the argument
emotion supplements rather than replaces the quantitative case

title: Rain dance and drought end
question: Does the writer's endorsement of the elders' claim commit the post hoc ergo propter hoc fallacy? Answer yes or no.
input: A travel writer reports: 'The village elders performed the rain dance on Saturday evening. By Tuesday, a thunderstorm broke the eight-month drought. The dance, the elders insist, called the rains—and the timing supports their view.' The writer notes meteorologists had been tracking a Pacific moisture surge for ten days that was forecast to reach the region midweek, but the writer dismisses this as 'coincidence' without elaboration.

must_identify: identifies rain dance as asserted cause and rainfall as effect
notes the justification is temporal sequence
notes the meteorological alternative was mentioned but dismissed without grounds
notes dismissal without reasoning does not count as ruling out alternatives

title: Tax cut and job growth
question: Does the press release commit the post hoc ergo propter hoc fallacy? Answer yes or no.
input: A senator's press release: 'I voted for the corporate tax cut in January. By December, the state added 40,000 jobs—the strongest year in a decade. The math is simple: cut taxes, create jobs.' The release does not mention the national economic expansion that added jobs in 47 other states, the new auto plant whose construction began two years prior, or the demographic surge of millennials entering peak employment age.

must_identify: identifies tax cut as asserted cause and job growth as effect
notes only temporal sequence is offered as justification
lists alternative explanations (national expansion, auto plant, demographics)
notes no comparative or mechanistic analysis

title: Insomnia and herbal tea
question: Does the wellness post commit the post hoc ergo propter hoc fallacy? Answer yes or no.
input: A wellness post claims: 'I drank valerian tea every night for two weeks and my insomnia disappeared by day ten. Valerian works.' Compare with a clinical statement: 'In a double-blind crossover trial, valerian extract reduced sleep latency by 14 minutes versus placebo (p<0.01); GABAergic activity is the proposed mechanism.' Only the first is being evaluated.

must_identify: identifies valerian tea as asserted cause and insomnia resolution as effect in the post
notes the post relies only on personal temporal sequence
notes no control, blinding, or mechanism in the post (the clinical statement is a distractor)
distinguishes the post from the clinical evidence and evaluates only the post

title: Bridge collapse investigation
question: Does this report commit the post hoc ergo propter hoc fallacy? Answer yes or no.
input: An engineering report concludes: 'The Pier 4 footing settled by 12cm in March; the bridge deck developed structural cracks in April and partially collapsed in May. We attribute the collapse to the foundation settlement. Finite-element modeling shows that 12cm of differential settlement at Pier 4 produces stress concentrations exceeding the deck's tensile capacity at the observed crack locations. Wind loading and traffic overload were measured and fell within design limits during the period.'

must_identify: identifies settlement as asserted cause and collapse as effect
notes engineering mechanism (FEM, stress concentration) is provided
notes alternatives (wind, traffic) were measured and ruled out
concludes the argument exceeds mere temporal sequence

title: Streak after coaching change
question: Does the columnist's argument fit the post hoc ergo propter hoc pattern? Answer yes or no.
input: A sports columnist writes: 'The Falcons fired coach Reyes on October 3rd. Since then, they've won six straight. Interim coach Voss has clearly turned the team around—the timing tells the whole story.' The column does not mention that star quarterback Davies returned from injury October 5th, that the six wins came against the four worst defenses in the league, or that the team's underlying performance metrics (yards per play, turnover differential) have not changed.

must_identify: identifies coaching change as asserted cause and win streak as effect
notes the argument relies on timing alone
lists alternatives (QB return, weak opponents, unchanged underlying metrics)
notes no mechanism or controlled comparison offered

title: Encryption standard endorsement
question: Identify the reasoning flaw in the consultant's argument.
input: A security consultant writes: 'Standard ZK-9 is cryptographically secure. The recommendation to adopt it comes from the National Cipher Board, whose recommendations are authoritative because they only endorse cryptographically secure standards. Therefore ZK-9 is secure, since the Board recommends it.' Independent academic cryptanalysis of ZK-9 has been conducted but is not cited in the consultant's argument.

must_identify: conclusion: ZK-9 is secure
premise: Board recommends it
Board's authority defined by endorsing only secure standards
independent cryptanalysis exists but is not used
the argument as written closes a loop

title: Novel as literary masterpiece
question: Does the critic's argument commit circular reasoning?
input: A critic declares: 'Halward's novel Ember Lattice is a masterpiece because masterpieces stand the test of time, and Ember Lattice will surely stand the test of time, as masterpieces invariably do.' The critic notes the book sold 40,000 copies in its first year and was shortlisted for the Brennan Prize, but uses these only to introduce the novel rather than to ground the masterpiece claim.

must_identify: conclusion: Ember Lattice is a masterpiece
premise: it will stand the test of time
that premise rests on it being a masterpiece
sales and shortlist mentioned only as introduction
no independent grounding for the masterpiece claim

title: Vaccine schedule recommendation
question: Does the committee's argument for the schedule commit circular reasoning?
input: A pediatric committee writes: 'The revised six-dose schedule reduces serious infection rates in children under five. A multi-site cohort study followed 8,400 children over four years, finding hospitalization rates 41% lower in the revised-schedule group compared to the prior schedule, with confidence interval [33%, 49%]. Some parents in online forums also report feeling more confident about the new schedule.'

must_identify: conclusion: revised schedule reduces serious infections
premise: cohort study showing lower hospitalization rates
study evidence is external to the conclusion
parent confidence is anecdotal, not used as proof
no premise presupposes the conclusion

title: Ancient law's legitimacy
question: What flaw does the scholar's legitimacy argument exhibit?
input: A scholar argues: 'The Edict of Vorn is legitimate law because it was issued by a legitimate sovereign. Vorn was a legitimate sovereign because his authority to issue binding edicts—including the Edict of Vorn—was recognized as valid.' The scholar references that Vorn ruled for 31 years and built three aqueducts, facts presented as historical color rather than as grounds for legitimacy.

must_identify: conclusion: the Edict is legitimate law
premise: Vorn was a legitimate sovereign
Vorn's legitimacy grounded in authority to issue the very Edict
reign length and aqueducts are historical color
loop between sovereign legitimacy and edict legitimacy

title: Two arguments to rank
question: Which argument exhibits circular reasoning, A or B?
input: Argument A: 'Telekinesis is real because reliable people have reported it, and these people are reliable because they would only report something real like telekinesis.' Argument B: 'Telekinesis is real because in 47 controlled laboratory trials at Wexler University, subjects moved a 2-gram pendulum more than chance would predict (p<0.01).' Both arguments conclude that telekinesis is real, but use very different supporting structures to reach that conclusion.

must_identify: both share the same conclusion
A's premise about reliable witnesses depends on telekinesis being real
B's premise cites independent experimental data
only A closes a justification loop
B may have other issues but is not circular

title: Tech conference attendees coding
question: What specific gap makes the recruiter's leap unjustified — sample size, selection bias, or both?
input: At a three-day JavaScript conference in San Francisco, a recruiter chatted with about twenty attendees during coffee breaks. Nineteen said they prefer functional programming styles. Back at her firm, she briefs leadership: 'Software developers worldwide overwhelmingly favor functional programming. We need to overhaul our hiring rubric to match what the global developer community wants.' She has not consulted any industry survey and bases the recommendation entirely on the coffee-break conversations.

must_identify: claim covers software developers worldwide
sample of twenty is far too small
attendees of a JavaScript conference are self-selected and unrepresentative
both size and selection bias undermine the inference

title: Grandfather and chain smoking
question: Does Luis's argument commit hasty generalization? Answer yes or no.
input: At a family dinner, Luis argues that warnings about smoking are exaggerated. 'My grandfather smoked two packs a day for sixty years and lived to ninety-three. Smoking clearly doesn't shorten lifespan — the medical establishment has been lying to us for decades, and any honest look at the evidence will show smokers live just as long as anyone else.' His cousin, a nurse, tries to push back, but Luis insists his grandfather's case settles the matter once and for all.

must_identify: claim is about smokers in general / population lifespan
evidence is a single anecdote (his grandfather)
n=1 cannot support a population-level conclusion
outliers exist in any distribution and don't refute aggregate trends

title: Two flawed inferences ranked
question: Which argument is the clearer example of hasty generalization, A or B?
input: Consider two arguments. Argument A: 'I called customer service at TelCo twice this month and was put on hold for over an hour each time. TelCo has the worst customer service of any phone company in the country — every customer suffers like I did.' Argument B: 'TelCo's stock price dropped the day after the CEO wore a red tie to the shareholder meeting. Clearly, the red tie caused investors to panic and dump their shares.' A media literacy instructor asks her students to identify which argument is the clearer example of hasty generalization.

must_identify: Argument A makes a population-wide claim from two personal calls
Argument A fits the small-sample-to-broad-claim pattern
Argument B is a false cause (post hoc), not a generalization
skill constraints distinguish hasty generalization from false cause

title: Foreign exchange student impressions
question: Does the Carters' conclusion commit hasty generalization? Answer yes or no.
input: After hosting one foreign exchange student from Norway who happened to be exceptionally tidy, the Carter family tells their neighbors: 'Norwegians are the cleanest people on earth. Every single one of them keeps an immaculate home — it must be cultural. We're convinced now.' The Carters have never visited Norway, hosted any other Norwegian, or read about Norwegian household habits. They base the entire claim on the behavior of their one teenage guest, Henrik, who stayed with them for ten months.

must_identify: claim covers all Norwegians
evidence is a single individual
n=1 cannot support a national-cultural generalization
Henrik's tidiness may be a personal trait, not a cultural one

title: Meta-analysis of clinical trials
question: Does the lead author's stated conclusion commit hasty generalization? Answer yes or no.
input: A team of researchers performs a meta-analysis pooling 62 randomized controlled trials of a new blood-pressure drug, covering more than 140,000 patients across 19 countries. The pooled analysis shows a small but statistically significant reduction in systolic pressure. The lead author concludes in the abstract: 'Across diverse adult populations, the drug produces a modest reduction in systolic blood pressure.' A skeptical commentator on social media accuses the authors of overgeneralizing from limited data and demands a retraction, calling the conclusion reckless.

must_identify: evidence base is 62 RCTs and 140,000+ patients across 19 countries
scope of claim ('diverse adult populations') matches the sample
sample is large and representative
the social media accusation is the trap; it does not reflect a real sampling flaw

title: Insider trading detector
question: Which reasoning flaw best describes the compliance officer's conclusion?
input: A regulator's algorithm flags potential insider trades with 97% sensitivity and a 1% false-positive rate. Estimates suggest only about 1 in 5,000 trades on the exchange is actually based on insider information. The algorithm flags trader Patel's transaction. The compliance officer announces: 'Given the algorithm's 97% accuracy, we will refer this trade for prosecution as an insider trade.'

must_identify: the flag is the case-specific evidence
the prior (1 in 5,000) is stated and very low
1% false positives over the 4,999 clean trades yield many false flags per real one

title: Soil contamination quick test
question: Does the consultant's reasoning exhibit base-rate neglect? Answer yes or no.
input: An environmental consultant explains to a developer: 'This field kit detects arsenic above safe limits 90% of the time when arsenic is present and gives a false positive 8% of the time when it isn't. In this region's soils, prior surveys indicate roughly 35% of plots exceed the safe limit. Plot 19 tested positive, so combining the prior and the test, there is a strong case — about 86% — that plot 19 is contaminated, but a lab confirmation is still warranted.'

must_identify: case-specific evidence is plot 19's positive field test
the 35% prior is explicitly stated
the consultant explicitly combines prior and test accuracy
the posterior is computed rather than assumed equal to test accuracy

title: Counterfeit currency scanner
question: Does the branch policy's reasoning exhibit base-rate neglect? Answer yes or no.
input: A bank's bill scanner identifies counterfeit notes with 99% accuracy in both directions. Federal Reserve data put the share of counterfeits in circulation at about 1 in 10,000 notes. When teller Naomi's scanner beeps on a $100 bill, branch policy — set after Bayesian analysis last quarter — directs her to set the note aside for verification rather than treat it as confirmed counterfeit, since most beeps in normal circulation are false alarms.

must_identify: case-specific evidence is the scanner beep
the prior (1 in 10,000) is stated and very low
policy explicitly accounts for the prior via Bayesian analysis
treating beep as preliminary, not conclusive, is correct use of the prior

title: Rare bird call identification
question: Which cognitive bias does the newsletter's announcement display?
input: An automated birdcall classifier identifies the endangered Pictish warbler with 94% sensitivity and a 3% false-positive rate per recording. Long-term censuses show the warbler appears in only about 1 of every 4,000 forest recordings made in the region. After the classifier tags clip 882 as a Pictish warbler, the conservation society's newsletter announces: 'Because our classifier is 94% accurate, we have confirmed a new sighting of the Pictish warbler in clip 882.'

must_identify: the classifier tag is the case-specific evidence
the prior (1 in 4,000) is stated and very low
3% false positives in the vast non-warbler majority dwarf true positives
announcement ignores the prior and uses only accuracy

title: Two analysts on fraud alert
question: Which analyst's reasoning better avoids base-rate neglect — A or B?
input: A bank's fraud model flags transactions with 95% sensitivity and a 2% false-positive rate; only about 1 in 1,000 transactions is actually fraudulent. Transaction T is flagged. Analyst A says: 'The model is 95% accurate, so T is almost certainly fraud — freeze the account.' Analyst B says: 'Given fraud is rare, even with 95% accuracy most flags are false; let's investigate before freezing.'

must_identify: both analysts see the same flag (case-specific evidence)
the 1-in-1,000 prior is stated
Analyst A relies only on the 95% accuracy

title: Tornado season chance estimate
question: Does Caleb's probability estimate exemplify the availability heuristic? Answer yes or no.
input: After two tornadoes touch down within fifty miles in a single week—both shown repeatedly on local news with dramatic footage—Caleb tells his wife the chance of a tornado hitting their property this season is 'easily one in three.' She points to the NOAA Storm Prediction Center's historical data for their county: roughly 0.4% annual probability of a tornado within one mile of any given point, with no upward trend this year. Caleb says he doesn't trust averages when he 'just saw two with his own eyes.'

must_identify: Caleb estimates tornado probability from two recently witnessed events
NOAA historical data contradicts his one-in-three estimate
vivid news footage and recency drive ease of recall

title: Two reasoning errors compared
question: Which reasoner's error is best characterized as the availability heuristic—A or B?
input: Reasoner A: After her cousin survived a car crash unbelted while another belted friend died, Mira concludes seatbelts make accidents more dangerous. She ignores NHTSA data showing belted occupants have 45% lower fatality rates. Reasoner B: After reading three magazine articles about shark attacks in Florida, Diego tells his family that swimming in Florida is now extremely dangerous and proposes they vacation in Maine instead. He cannot cite any base rate but says, 'I keep reading about these attacks.' ISAF data shows Florida shark attack rates are unchanged from prior years and remain below 1 per million beach visits.

must_identify: Reasoner B's risk judgment is driven by ease of recalling articles
B shows mismatch between recalled examples and stable ISAF base rate
Reasoner A's error is generalizing from a small sample / anecdote, not specifically frequency-from-recall against media salience
